title: Range Queries & Advanced Data Structures
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs repeatedly test choosing and implementing the right precomputed structure so many range queries beat naive linear scans.

phases.goal: Establish the precompute-once trade-off and the decision guide for which range-query structure to reach for.

must_hit.point: A recurring trade-off is precomputing a structure once so many queries answer in O(log n) or O(1) instead of naive O(n) per query.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts one-time build cost against repeated linear scans over the same array.

must_hit.point: Decision guide: immutable + associative query → prefix sums; immutable + idempotent query (min/max/gcd) → sparse table; point update + prefix/range sum → Fenwick Tree; range update + range query → Segment Tree with lazy propagation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps immutability, update type, and query type to the four structures without conflating them.

must_hit.point: For an immutable array, range sum [L, R] is the prefix sum up to R minus the prefix sum up to L-1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the prefix[R] − prefix[L−1] identity (or equivalent 1-based indexing).

must_hit.point: Difference-array trick: to add v on [L, R], add v at diff[L] and subtract v at diff[R+1], then one prefix-sum pass yields final values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes O(1) range updates on an initially empty array followed by a single reconstruction via prefix sums.

probes: When would you reach for prefix sums versus a Fenwick Tree versus a Segment Tree for range queries?
How do you answer a range sum on an immutable array after a linear preprocess?

hints.1: Think about whether the array changes and what kind of updates you need.
hints.2: Match immutability and associative vs idempotent queries to the lightest structure, then escalate to BIT or segment tree when updates appear.
hints.3: Immutable associative → prefix; immutable idempotent min/max/gcd → sparse table; point update + sum → BIT; range update + range query → lazy segment tree.

phases.goal: Check that the candidate can explain how sparse tables, BITs, and segment trees (including lazy propagation) actually answer queries and updates.

must_hit.point: A sparse table stores answers for every power-of-two length; for length L, RMQ uses two overlapping blocks of size 2^k with 2^k ≤ L, which is valid because min is idempotent, giving O(1) query with no updates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions power-of-two blocks, overlapping mins, and that sparse tables do not support updates.

must_hit.point: In a 1-indexed BIT, bit[i] stores the sum of a range ending at i whose length equals the lowest set bit of i; update does i += i & (-i) and prefix query does i -= i & (-i).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the low-bit trick and the opposite jump directions for update versus prefix sum.

must_hit.point: For i = 12 (binary 1100), the lowest set bit is 4 (0100), so bit[12] covers the sum of 4 elements ending at 12 (indices 9, 10, 11, 12).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks the binary example or an equivalent lowest-set-bit coverage explanation.

must_hit.point: A segment tree is a full binary tree of intervals; the root is [0, n-1], children split at mid, leaves are single elements, commonly stored in an array of size 4n; query returns a node value when fully inside the range, a neutral value when fully outside, else combines both children.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes recursive interval splitting, the 4n backing array, and the three query cases.

must_hit.point: Lazy propagation: on a fully covered node, update the node immediately and store the pending update in lazy[node] without visiting children; push the lazy value down only when children must be visited later, restoring O(log n) for both range updates and range queries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts updating every leaf versus deferring with lazy and push.

probes: How does a sparse table answer a range minimum in constant time?
Walk through how a Fenwick Tree uses i & (-i) for update and prefix sum.
What does lazy propagation store, and when do you push?

hints.1: Start from what each node or table entry stores, then how a query walks those entries.
hints.2: Sparse table: two overlapping power-of-two mins; BIT: jump by lowest set bit; segment tree: fully in / fully out / split; lazy: mark and push on demand.
hints.3: st[L][k] and st[R−2^k+1][k] for RMQ; BIT update adds then i += i&(-i), query subtracts i -= i&(-i); lazy updates the covered node, writes lazy[node], and push applies pending adds to children before descending.

phases.goal: Force an explicit comparison of build/query/update cost and when the heavier structure is actually justified.

must_hit.point: Prefix sums: O(n) build, O(1) query, but updates are not supported in the immutable setting; BIT balances point update and prefix/range sum to O(log n) each.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts O(1) immutable prefix queries against O(n) rebuild/update cost versus BIT’s O(log n) for both.

must_hit.point: Sparse table builds in O(n log n) and queries in O(1); it is strictly superior to segment trees for immutable RMQ when query volume is massive, but does not support updates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers sparse table over segment tree for static RMQ and notes the no-update limitation.

must_hit.point: A BIT needs only an array of size n+1 and has smaller constant factors than a segment tree; a segment tree commonly uses about 4n space but is more versatile across operations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites BIT space n+1 versus segment tree ~4n and versatility of changing the combine operation.

must_hit.point: Without lazy propagation, a range update on a segment tree would take O(n log n) by touching leaves; use lazy segment tree only when you truly need both arbitrary range updates and arbitrary range queries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains why lazy exists and when to avoid reaching for it.

probes: When is a sparse table better than a segment tree for RMQ?
Why prefer a BIT over a segment tree for point-update range sums?
When is lazy propagation actually necessary?

hints.1: Compare whether the array is immutable and whether you need range updates.
hints.2: Immutable idempotent RMQ favors sparse table; point updates favor BIT for sums; both range update and range query need lazy segment tree.
hints.3: Sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) query, no updates; BIT: size n+1, O(log n) update/query; lazy only when both range update and range query are required.

phases.goal: Apply the structures to a non-obvious problem shape and to interview tool-selection discipline.

must_hit.point: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self: iterate right to left; query the BIT for how many seen values are strictly smaller, then add 1 at the current value’s index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes right-to-left processing with query-then-update on a frequency BIT.

must_hit.point: Values may be negative or extremely large (e.g. 10^4 or 10^9), so they cannot be BIT indices directly; coordinate-compress unique sorted values to dense ranks starting at 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate insists on coordinate compression before indexing the BIT.

must_hit.point: In interviews, pick the lightest tool that fits: prefix sums before BIT before segment tree; many hard OA stories are a standard structure (e.g. BIT for counting inversions) behind verbose wording.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps requested operations to the lightest structure rather than defaulting to a full segment tree.

probes: How would you count smaller elements to the right of each index using a BIT?
What goes wrong if you use raw array values as Fenwick indices?
Given a verbose OA story, how do you decide among prefix sums, BIT, and segment tree?

hints.1: Process elements in an order that turns “to the right” into “already seen.”
hints.2: Right-to-left: query rank−1 for count of smaller, then add 1 at the compressed rank; compress because values may be negative or huge.
hints.3: Sort unique values, map to 1..m, walk i from n−1 to 0, result[i]=query(rank−1), add(rank,1); prefer prefix → BIT → segment tree, and lazy only for true range update + range query.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefix sums give O(n) build and O(1) range sum on an immutable array, but a point change forces an O(n) rebuild; a BIT makes both point update and prefix/range sum O(log n).

tradeoffs.topic: Sparse table vs Segment Tree for RMQ
tradeoffs.strong_answer: For immutable RMQ, a sparse table builds in O(n log n) and answers in O(1) via two overlapping power-of-two mins because min is idempotent, and is strictly superior when query volume is massive; a segment tree supports point updates in O(log n) but is slower per static query and needs roughly 4n space.

A BIT uses an array of size n+1 with small constants and shines for point update + prefix/range sum; a segment tree uses about 4n space but adapts to min/max/gcd and, with lazy propagation, to range updates plus range queries.

tradeoffs.topic: Difference array vs Lazy Segment Tree
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Difference arrays give O(1) range adds when all updates come before a single reconstruction via prefix sums; if you interleave arbitrary range updates with arbitrary range queries, you need a segment tree with lazy propagation for O(log n) per operation.

gotchas.trap: Using a sparse table (or plain prefix sums) when the array must support updates.
gotchas.correction: Sparse tables and immutable prefix structures do not support updates; switch to a BIT for point-update sums or a segment tree (with lazy if range updates are required).

gotchas.trap: Using raw nums values—possibly negative or as large as 10^4 or 10^9—directly as BIT indices.
gotchas.correction: Coordinate-compress: map the smallest unique value to 1, the next to 2, and so on, so ranks fit a dense array of size ≤ n.

gotchas.trap: Reaching for a segment tree with lazy propagation when only point updates or only a final-query-after-updates pattern is needed.
gotchas.correction: Prefer prefix sums, then BIT, then a plain segment tree; use lazy only when you truly need both arbitrary range updates and arbitrary range queries.

gotchas.trap: Assuming two overlapping sparse-table blocks work for non-idempotent queries like sum.
gotchas.correction: Overlapping power-of-two blocks are safe for idempotent ops such as min/max/gcd; for associative but non-idempotent ops like sum, use prefix sums (immutable) or a tree that combines disjoint segments.
